newsitem.title: USA: Fed policy-makers warn of risk of higher inflation.
newsitem.headline: Fed policy-makers warn of risk of higher inflation.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
Federal Reserve policy-makers warned on Wednesday of the risk of higher inflation and left open the possibility that the central bank may raise interest rates at some point in the future.

Echoing comments made on Tuesday by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan and repeated by him again on Wednesday, the policy-makers described the economy's performance as outstanding but said the Fed needed to be vigilant to try to make sure that continues.

"The economy as a whole is functioning amazingly well," Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin told the House Banking Committee. "The overriding objective -- shared by all participants in the economy -- is to keep the good news flowing."

Speaking to a subcommittee of the House Banking panel on Tuesday, Greenspan called the recent combination of strong economic growth and low inflation "exceptional." He repeated that testimony to the Senate Banking Committee Wednesday.

Stock prices, which rallied on Tuesday as investors concluded from Greenspan's comments that the Fed was not set to raise short-term interest rates right away, moved further into record territory on Wednesday. The Dow Jones industrial average added 44.13 points to 8,105.78.

To ensure that the economic good times continue, Fed Governor Laurence Meyer told the House Banking Committee that the central bank needed to be vigilant to prevent the economy from overheating and stoking up inflation.
"At the very good growth rate that we have now, what we want to avoid doing is getting into a boom-bust cycle," added New York Fed President Wlliam McDonough.
Rivlin, McDonough and Meyer are all members of the central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee, which is headed by Greenspan.
Rivlin told the lawmakers that all the FOMC members agree that the risk of faster inflation now was "somewhat greater" than the risk of a recession.

"There seems to be little risk of the economy slowing down too much in the near term and sliding into recession," she said. "The risks seem higher on the other side -- that many of the factors holding down inflationary pressures will prove temporary."

In a bid to keep inflation in check and thus lengthen the economic expansion, the Fed raised short-term rates in March for the first time in more than two years, bumping them up a quarter percentage point. It has since held rates steady.

In deciding whether to raise rates again, policy-makers must weigh the risk of slowing the economy unnecessarily against possibly waiting too long, which could lead to an overheated economy and rising prices and wages, Rivlin said.
"It's a tough call," she said.
Meyer said the economy seems to have slowed to a more sustainable pace after a burst of growth in the first quarter, adding he expects growth to remain moderate through 1998.
The economy grew at a 5.9 percent rate in the first quarter, the fastest pace in more than nine years and well above what economists say is sustainable without fuelling inflation.

Meyer voiced fears that the economy is running at a level that could lead to inflation next year. With the unemployment rate at 5 percent, it is already below the 5-1/2 percent level that Meyer said can be maintained without pushing up wages and fanning inflation.

In his semi-annual report to Congress this week, Greenspan said that Fed policy-makers were "reasonably confident" that inflation will be quite modest this year. But, he added, they see faster inflation next year.
Wholesale prices have fallen for a record six straight months, while consumer prices have risen so far this year at the slowest pace since 1986.
Besides hearing from Rivlin, McDonough and Meyer, the House Banking Committee took testimony on Fed policy from business and union representatives, Wall Street experts and academics.

Gordon Richards, economist for the National Association of Manufacturers, urged the Fed to hold rates steady to accommodate growth. "The best course of action for the Federal Reserve (would be to) simply leave interest rates the way they are," he said.
Professor James Galbraith of the University of Texas agreed. "Since evidence does not show accelerating inflation, the prudent course is to take as little action as possible," he told the committee.
